passage:
Tenzin, sit with your Ganga aunty a minute. You remind me of myself at twenty-five, watching someone the way you're watching Sonam now. Mine was Prakash, at the tea company office in Siliguri. He took every late shift, ate lunch over spreadsheets, stopped coming to our Saturday badminton. He got promoted twice in a year.
I'll be honest, first I was jealous. Then one evening I saw him fall asleep sitting up at his desk, pen still in his hand, and the jealousy just went.
I didn't lecture him about balance. I said, 'I'm getting momos at seven. Come for twenty minutes, then go back to your work.' He came. He laughed for the first time in weeks.
He still wanted the promotion, and he got it. But he came every Thursday after that.

qa.q: What did Prakash stop coming to?
qa.a: Our Saturday badminton, as Ganga puts it.

qa.q: What made Ganga's jealousy of Prakash turn into concern?
qa.a: Seeing him fall asleep sitting up at his desk, pen still in his hand, showed how worn out he was, and the jealousy went.

qa.q: What choice did Ganga make instead of lecturing Prakash, and why did it work?
qa.a: She invited him for momos for twenty minutes and told him to go back to his work after, offering a break without questioning his goals.

qa.q: What might Prakash have felt when invited for just twenty minutes?
qa.a: Prakash may have felt relieved and cared for, since the invitation respected his work instead of criticising it.

grounding: Shows a colleague who sees a peer giving up sleep and friendships for promotion, moves from envy to concern, and offers a break without judging his goals.

passage:
Rain had flooded the lane outside the insurance office, and half the staff had gone home early. Deepak hadn't. Minakshi found him at eight, still at his desk, eyes red, three empty tea cups lined up by the keyboard. He had skipped his cousin's engagement last Sunday to finish the quarterly report, and he'd missed every team lunch since March.
Minakshi felt a twist of envy first. The regional head praised him in every meeting. Then she noticed his hand shaking as he reached for a fourth cup.
She sat on the edge of the next desk. 'I'm not telling you to stop going for team lead. You'd be good. But the water's rising and the last bus leaves at nine. I'll take the claims file tomorrow morning. Go home and sleep tonight?'
He looked at the window, then at her, and slowly saved his work.

qa.q: What did Deepak skip last Sunday to finish the quarterly report?
What did Minakshi feel first, and what changed it?
qa.a: She felt a twist of envy because the regional head praised him, then concern when she noticed his hand shaking as he reached for more tea.

qa.q: Which choice by Minakshi made the offer easy for Deepak to accept?
qa.a: She said she wasn't asking him to stop going for team lead and offered to take the claims file, so the break didn't question his goal.

qa.q: How might Deepak feel hearing 'You'd be good' from a colleague?
qa.a: He might feel seen and less defensive, since his ambition was respected rather than judged.

grounding: Shows a colleague watching a peer sacrifice sleep and relationships for promotion, setting aside envy and offering a break out of genuine concern.
